newsitem.title: UK: Derivative market downplays UK poll--at its peril?.
newsitem.headline: Derivative market downplays UK poll--at its peril?.

text.p: British debt derivatives may be taking a little too much for granted, some specialists say.

By Wednesday, with one day to go before an election, there were few signs of investors actively hedging for anything other than market serenity as a victory by the opposition Labour Party was so well expected.
But analysts said that relying on a post-poll slide in volatility could be unwise. The interest rate outlook could come into sharper focus once the election is out of the way.

"There's a feeling this time that the election is a foregone conclusion, and afterwards there is nothing to keep volatility up," said Ian Aubrey head of futures and options sales at Yamaichi in London.
"But I would not be short of volatility going into this."

Usually, an event as potentially tumultuous as the end of a long-period of power for one party -- the Conservatives have been in government since 1979 -- would send investors scurrying to the market to hedge against the outcome.
But in stark contrast to the leadup to the 1992 election volatility, which reflects market expectations of the likelihood of major price movements, has stayed relatively stable.
Implied volatility of short sterling options rose to more than 50 percent before the last election, which compares to a current level of nine percent.

"Volatility is stunningly steady in the face of this election," said a trader at a major European bank here. "It's hard to find anyone who's worried about this, and even harder to persuade them that they should hedge."
Traders said Labour has so successfully shed its tax and spend image, and has been so far ahead in the polls for so long, that any vestiges of fear have evaporated.
The latest opinion poll, conducted by Gallup, gave Labour a lead of 22 points over the Conservatives.
"Labour are seen as closet Conservatives," said Andy Ash, derivatives analyst at Monument Derivatives. "A Labour victory looks as though it would have no effect on the market."
Ash said the short-end would be interesting as there was uncertainty about whether interest rates would rise a quarter or half a percentage point from the current 6.0 percent.
Aubrey said positioning had increased ahead of the election, with much of the activity based on picking up gilts while they appeared cheap.
He said gilt options volatility, hovering around 8.0 percent at the moment, could head as high as 10 or 11 percent. "It's a smart play to be long of gilt volatility," he said.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at the Cooperative Bank in London, said there were few signs the election was doing anything to volatility.
"Most people are flat going into this," he said. "There isn't any panic because it looks like the outcome is well-known. A scenario of a 60-to-100 seat majority is priced in."
However, he said there was only limited downside for options volatility, particularly since U.S. non-farm payrolls data were scheduled to be released the day after the British election.
Traders also said volumes in British debt derivatives have suffered from an image problem, in the wake of high-profile scandals such as the Barings debacle.
According to data from the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange short sterling options volume in 1996 fell 34 percent, while gilt options dipped 22 percent.
Last month, gilt options trade was down almost 35 percent on February. Short sterling options trade was down some 24 percent.
"If there is any outcome other than a significant Labour majority, a lot of people are going to wish they had been better hedged," said a trader at a British brokerage.
